explanations.explanation: Paul, who is writing this letter from his chains, says his circumstances “…have actually served to advance the gospel.” Chains, and he calls it progress. Most of us would send in a complaint. Paul sends in a progress report.

Hinder is a fair guess, friend, because chains look like a roadblock to everybody. But Paul, who is writing this letter from those chains, says his circumstances “…have actually served to advance the gospel.” I think he knows how surprising that sounds, and he says it anyway.

Divide sounds like trouble, but it's not the word Paul picks. Paul, the one writing this letter in chains, says his circumstances “…have actually served to advance the gospel.” He does talk about people with envy and rivalry later on, and even there he says Christ is preached. So the chains and the drama didn't stop a thing.

Paul says, “…it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ.” The whole palace guard, friend. That news traveled farther than a rumor at a family reunion. And he says it reached everyone else too.

That's an easy one to swap, since a guard is a guard. But Paul says the palace guard, not the temple guard. He says it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard “…and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ.” One little word changes the whole building.

The Sanhedrin was the council of Jewish leaders (Acts 5:21), so it's a big name to reach for. But Paul doesn't name them here. He says it has become clear throughout “…the whole palace guard and to everyone else…” So the news got out, and it got out wide.

I get why you'd think so, because chains are scary and quiet feels safe. But the verse says the opposite. Most of the brothers, “…confident in the Lord by my chains, now dare more greatly to speak the word without fear.” Paul's chains turned into a pep talk.

False it is. Paul says most of the brothers are “…confident in the Lord by my chains, now dare more greatly to speak the word without fear.” So nobody went quiet. The chains made them braver, and I'd love to see that on a motivational poster.

Paul says, “…some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill.” So the same Christ gets preached from two very different places in the heart. It's like two cookie tables side by side at the same event, and one of them keeps counting the other's line. Paul doesn't hide it, he just names it.

Fear and doubt are common troubles, but Paul doesn't name them here. He says some preach Christ “…out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill.” Back in verse 14 he says most of the brothers speak the word without fear. So fear isn't what he points to for this group.

Those are heavy feelings, but they're not the ones Paul picks. He says some preach Christ “…out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill.” Paul gives us exactly two words for the other group, and they're envy and rivalry. Stick with what the text says, friend.

Paul says, “The latter do so in love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel.” So these folks aren't just preaching, they're preaching in love. And they know what Paul is appointed to do. That's a good group to have in your corner.

Fear is close to the opposite of what Paul says here. In verse 14, the brothers dare to speak the word without fear. And in verse 16 he says the goodwill group does it “…in love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel.” Love is the word that fills the blank.

Secret makes for a good spy movie, but it's not in the verse. Paul says they preach Christ “…in love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel.” Nothing about sneaking around. These folks are out in the open, and that's the point of preaching.

explanations.answer: Add to the distress of his chains
explanations.explanation: Paul says the insincere preachers are “…supposing that they can add to the distress of my chains.” Notice the word supposing. That's what they think will happen, not what Paul says does happen. Paul's already in chains, and they figure they can pile something on top.

That's a believable plan, but it's not in the text. Paul says they preach Christ out of selfish ambition, “…supposing that they can add to the distress of my chains.” The verse stays right on his chains. We don't need to add a bigger scheme than the one Paul names.

I can see why that one sounds right, since chains and distance go together in a lot of stories. But Paul never says that here. He says they suppose “…they can add to the distress of my chains.” The only thing the text says they aim at is his distress.

True. Paul asks, “What then is the issue?” and then answers it himself: “Just this: that in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached.” He cuts through all the drama like a man who's already done the math. What matters to him is that Christ is preached.

I think the question made it sound like a trap, but this one's True. Paul asks, “What then is the issue?” and he says, “Just this: that in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached.” He answers his own question without even leaving the verse. So the card matches the text word for word.

Paul says, “And in this I rejoice.” That's right after he admits some people preach with false motives. Most of us would be stewing in that situation. Paul looks at Christ being preached and picks joy.

Grief would be a natural feeling after hearing about people with false motives. But Paul says, “And in this I rejoice.” He's pointing at Christ being preached, not at the people's motives. So the blank gets a happier word than grieves.

I'll worry over a batch of cookies cooling on the counter, but Paul doesn't go there. He says, “And in this I rejoice.” The thing he's looking at is that Christ is preached, whether by false motives or true. Worry doesn't get a seat at that table.
Paul says, “…my distress will turn out for my deliverance.” Notice he says he knows it, not that he hopes it. That's a big statement from a man in chains. His distress doesn't get the last word.

Downfall sounds like where distress usually heads, friend. But Paul says the opposite: “…my distress will turn out for my deliverance.” He says he knows it, too. So the blank wants a word with hope in it.

Punishment is a heavy word, and I understand why it came to mind with chains in the picture. But Paul says, “…my distress will turn out for my deliverance.” That's the word he writes. And he's got a lot of confidence about it.

explanations.answer: Their prayers and the Spirit's provision
explanations.explanation: Paul says it will come “…through your prayers and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.” So the Philippians are part of this, even from far away. Prayer doesn't need a stamp or a delivery truck. And the Spirit's provision is right there next to it.

explanations.answer: Their gifts and the guards' kindness
explanations.explanation: Gifts and kindness are nice things, but Paul doesn't list them here. He says, “…through your prayers and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.” The guards aren't named as part of his deliverance. The two things are prayers and the Spirit's provision.

explanations.answer: His defense and the court's mercy
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a plan a lawyer would write down. But Paul doesn't say it that way. He says his deliverance comes “…through your prayers and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.” Nothing about the court's mercy in the verse.

I can see why you'd read it that way, since staying alive makes the exalting easier to picture. But Paul says Christ will be exalted in his body “…whether by life or by death.” Both are covered. So it's not only if he keeps on living.
False, friend. Paul says he hopes “…now as always Christ will be exalted in my body, whether by life or by death.” That's both options, not just one. Either way, he wants Christ lifted up.

explanations.answer: He says he does not know
explanations.explanation: Paul asks, “So what shall I choose?” and then answers, “I do not know.” That's an honest answer. He's like a man with two good options and no coin to flip. Paul doesn't pretend to have it all figured out.

explanations.answer: He says the church should decide
explanations.explanation: Handing it to the church would be a neat answer, but Paul doesn't give it. He asks, “So what shall I choose?” and then says, “I do not know.” The church isn't named as the decider anywhere in the verse. He just lets the question sit.

explanations.answer: He says the court will decide it
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a believable way for a man in chains to answer. But Paul doesn't mention a court deciding anything here. He asks, “So what shall I choose?” and then says, “I do not know.” The honest answer is the whole answer.
Paul says, “I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed.” Far better indeed, and he doesn't hold back on that. He's pointing at Christ as the reason.

I miss my six cookie cutter kids, so I know how strong that pull can be. But Paul doesn't name family here. He says, “I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed.” Christ is the one he names.

Being with other apostles sounds like a good time, but that's not what Paul writes. He says, “I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed.” He doesn't mention the apostles in this verse at all. The answer is Christ, and Paul puts it right in the sentence.

Paul says, “But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body.” The "you" is the Philippians, the people he's writing to. So even though he calls departing far better, he keeps them in view. I think that's what a good friend does.

Timothy, who is named with Paul at the start of the letter (Philippians 1:1), is a good guess. But Paul says, “But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body.” He's speaking to the Philippians with that word "you.” Timothy isn't the one in this sentence.

Paul did just talk about the people who preach out of envy and rivalry, so they're fresh in mind. But he says, “But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body.” He's talking to the Philippians. His rivals aren't who he's pointing at.

True. Paul says, “Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and will continue with all of you for your progress and joy in the faith…” A verse earlier he said "I do not know," and now he says "I know." Keep up, friend.

I think the earlier "I do not know" threw you off, and I don't blame you. But this one is True. Paul says, “Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and will continue with all of you for your progress and joy in the faith…” He moves from torn to convinced.

explanations.answer: Live in a way worthy of the gospel
explanations.explanation: Paul says, “Nevertheless, conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ.” That's the big ask in one sentence. And he says whether he comes or only hears about them, he wants to know they stand firm. It's a plain request.

explanations.answer: Come and visit him in his chains
explanations.explanation: A visit would be kind, but that's not his ask. Paul says the visit would be going the other way: “…whether I come and see you or only hear about you in my absence…” His big ask is “…conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ.” He wants their living to match the gospel.

explanations.answer: Send Timothy to him right away
explanations.explanation: Timothy, who is named with Paul at the start of the letter (Philippians 1:1), doesn't come up in these verses at all. Paul's big ask is “…conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ.” Nothing about a rush trip. His ask is about how they live.

Paul wants to know they “…stand firm in one spirit…” and are contending together as one. It's like a whole batch coming out of the oven at once, all done together. One spirit, and they hold the line as one.

Custom is a neat guess, but Paul doesn't say it. He wants to know they “…stand firm in one spirit…” The standing firm is together, in one spirit, and he adds that they contend as one. Custom doesn't show up in the verse.
Law sounds like a serious word for a serious moment. But Paul says they “…stand firm in one spirit…” He's talking about being together in how they stand. Nothing about a law in this verse.

explanations.answer: The opponents' destruction and the Philippians' salvation
explanations.explanation: Paul says, “This is a clear sign of their destruction but of your salvation, and it is from God.” The sign points both ways, one for the opponents and one for the Philippians. And Paul says it's from God. That's the text, and I'll leave it there.

explanations.answer: The opponents' victory and the Philippians' defeat
explanations.explanation: Those two are flipped from what Paul writes. He says, “This is a clear sign of their destruction but of your salvation, and it is from God.” So for the Philippians it's a sign of salvation, not defeat. It's a heavy passage, but the sign is on their side.

explanations.answer: The opponents' strength and the Philippians' weakness
explanations.explanation: That might sound like what you'd expect from opposition. But Paul says, “This is a clear sign of their destruction but of your salvation, and it is from God.” Strength and weakness aren't the words he picks. He picks destruction and salvation.

Paul says, “…it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him…” It's a heavy verse, and I think it's one to sit with for a moment. He puts believing and suffering in the same sentence. Paul doesn't dress it up.

Speaking is a good fit with other parts of this passage, where the brothers dare to speak the word without fear. But this verse says, “…not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him…” So the blank gets a harder word than speak. I think it's worth reading that one slowly.

Work shows up in this passage when Paul talks about fruitful labor. But this verse says, “…not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him…” That's a heavier word than work. It's a part of the passage that's worth sitting with.

I can see why it might seem like theirs is a different road, since Paul's in chains and they're not. But Paul says, “…you are encountering the same struggle you saw I had, and now hear that I still have.” Same struggle, not a different one. So this one is False.

False, friend. Paul says, “…you are encountering the same struggle you saw I had, and now hear that I still have.” They saw his struggle, and they hear he's still in it. It's the same one, so they share it.
